newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Booming China life insurance mainly local.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Booming China life insurance mainly local.

text.p: China's life insurance market is expanding fast, especially in the booming east coast city of Shanghai, due to cutbacks in the social welfare system and rising incomes, industry analysts say.

But the market is still dominated by three domestic insurance companies, and foreign firms trying to establish a position in the lucrative trade are being forced to do so only at a snail's pace, they said.

The total premium income generated from life insurance services in China reached 33 billion yuan ($4 billion) last year, an increase of 70 percent over 1995, Xinhua news agency has reported, citing statistics from the Ping An Insurance Co.
Experts say China life insurance premiums are expected to reach 100 billion yuan by 2000.

In Shanghai alone, life insurance premiums reached 1.3 billion yuan in the first quarter of this year, a massive increase of 122.4 percent over the same period last year, the local Wen Hui Bao newspaper reported last month.
"China's life insurance market has developed at an amazing speed over the past few years, especially in Shanghai," said an official with the China Pacific Insurance Co Ltd.
"The reform of the social welfare system and rising income levels now offer a good opportunity for the development of life insurance," he added.

The per capita annual income of Chinese urban residents has increased at an average rate of five percent per year for the past five years, and last year reached about 4,500 yuan, official figures show.

As part of the move from state planning to a market-driven economy, the government is shifting some of the social welfare burden to companies and individuals, forcing them to pay a proportion of medical fees and pensions.

"Pensions provided by the government and companies are not enough to maintain a comfortable life after retirement," said an life insurance agent. "So people buy life insurance as an additional safeguard for their future."
Pension insurance is the most popular business, with many middle-aged people buying policies as a supplement to their government or company pensions, insurance agents said.
The average monthly premium for pension insurance is around 100 yuan, which, depending on the person's age, should yield around 2,600 yuan annual income after retirement, they said.

"The pension provided by the government can only maintain the basics of life. I bought pension insurance so that I can live more comfortably after retirement," said a 40-year-old man working for a state-owned enterprise.

The huge potential of China's life insurance business has attracted great attention from overseas firms, but the government is taking a very gradual approach to letting in foreign competition, industry analysts said.

The market is now dominated by the three state insurance companies -- the People's Insurance Co of China (PICC), China Pacific Insurance Co and Ping An Insurance Co. Together they control 97.14 percent of China's total life insurance market.

The market share of American International Assurance (AIA), the only foreign company licensed to write life insurance policies, was a flimsy 0.69 percent in 1995 and has grown little in the past two years, industry analysts said.
"When AIA entered China five years ago, they attracted customers with its completely new promotion methods," said an analyst with a local insurance company.
"But their business has not continued to expand so quickly because domestic companies have learned from them and have become more competitive," she said.
"Foreign companies are eager to join the market, but the government is taking a cautious attitude on licensing foreign firms to underwrite life insurance policies," the analyst said.
Since AIA opened shop in Shanghai in 1992, only one Sino-Canada joint venture called Zhong Hong Life Assurance has been allowed into the same market, late in 1996.
"Foreign firms have rich experience and the government is concerned that they may threaten the baby domestic insurance companies," said an official with a major local life insurance company.

"But we ourselves do not worry about their competition," he said. "Actually, the arrival of AIA brought China a completely new concept of handling the insurance business and they have done a lot to educate both local companies and residents."
